label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Úna set up this blog years ago so that the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds could keep up with us, and I’m glad of it now. There is something I need to tell everyone properly. Some of you have already heard, and some have heard only bits of it. That is my fault. I should have spoken sooner, and directly, instead of letting news travel ahead of me.

I have agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on **15 January 2027**. I’m putting that date here plainly because I don’t want anyone to hear it from somebody else again.

I know that will be hard news for some of you. It has been hard to write, though I have had longer to get used to it than you have. This is the old Mulkerrin place, near Oughterard, where Tom grew up, built by his grandfather Pádraig Mulkerrin in 1931. Nobody in this family needs to be told that it is more than a house. But it is a house as well, with a roof and pipes and damp and work that cannot be put off indefinitely. I have had to think about both things.

I want to explain why I am selling, what is being kept, and how we can have a day there together before it is cleared. I also want to say something about the way the news came out. I won’t pretend I handled that well.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It is forty minutes each way. That might not sound much, and on some days it isn’t. On other days I have found myself putting off leaving, then going because it needs to be done, then coming home tired in a way that doesn’t have much to do with driving.

There has been a comfort in having the house to go to. I don’t want to deny that now, simply because I have decided to sell it. It was somewhere I could still go and be in a place Tom had known all his life. For a while, the jobs themselves helped. There was something definite to do: get out there, open up, check everything, make sure all was well enough until the next visit.

But I have come to dread some of those visits, and I have not been honest with you about that.

Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I didn’t tell anybody. I am telling you now, which is probably not the easiest way to learn it either. At the time I thought that I had got up, I had managed, and there was no need to make a thing of it. I was embarrassed too. I had no wish to become the subject of a family discussion about whether I could be trusted to go out on my own.

That sounds stubborn when I write it down. It was stubborn.

The fall frightened me. It still frightens me. I am afraid of being alone at the house now, particularly when it is cold or the ground is bad. I don’t go out without thinking about that step and those twenty minutes. I am seventy-one. I am not incapable, but neither do I want to spend my time proving that I can keep doing something which has become too much for me.

I cannot go on maintaining the house. I should have said that before I reached the point of agreeing a sale. Instead, I kept going out, and when anyone asked, I gave them very little reason to think I was finding it difficult.

There are practical matters too, and they are substantial ones. Ó Flaithearta’s did the roof survey in September. The slates and the back chimney need work, and the quote was €38,000. That is before dealing with the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing to sell to anyone anyway.

I know a list of repairs can sound a poor answer to someone who is thinking about their father’s house, or their grandfather’s house. I am thinking about those things too. But the repairs do not disappear because the house matters to us. Nor does the responsibility for getting them done.

I don’t want to turn this into an account of every journey or every job, as though I have been keeping a tally against the family. I haven’t. I know people have their own homes, work, children and difficulties, and that Boston and Perth and Leeds are not just down the road. I am explaining what looking after Glenmore has become for me, not asking anyone to feel guilty for living elsewhere.

The buyers are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It is not going to be a holiday let.

That mattered to me. So did the price, of course, but it wasn’t the only thing that mattered. The price was fair. It was less than the Dublin crowd offered in the summer, and I took the lower offer on purpose. I wanted it to be someone’s home.

I cannot tell you how the Joyces will live there, and once the sale is complete it will be their house to make their own. I know that. There will be changes, and I expect some of them would take me a while to get used to. It would be foolish to sell a house and expect the next family to live around ours.

But knowing that children will be living there again has helped me.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I have thought of that often. I am not going to put words in his mouth beyond the ones he actually said, or claim that he has somehow settled every difficult part of this for us. He isn’t here to talk it over with, and I miss being able to do that. Still, he did say it, and it is something I can hold on to.

There is plenty I will miss about being able to go out to Glenmore whenever I choose. I will miss knowing that I can let myself in. I will miss being able to leave something there and find it in the same place next time. Those are ordinary things, but they are part of what makes a house yours, and I know I am giving them up.

And then there are the things no survey can account for.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. It was not a private occasion as far as the cattle were concerned. I can’t think of the place without thinking of that, and of the two of us before we knew most of what life was going to ask of us.

I have had that memory for nearly fifty years. I don’t expect it will become less clear because someone else has the keys. But I will miss being able to walk out behind the house without having to ask or explain myself.

I think too of the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan would refuse to come out until his lips were blue, as though we were only spoiling his enjoyment by suggesting he might be frozen. When I think of those days, I don’t think first about the work of looking after a house. I think of the children, and Tom, and how far away all this would have seemed to us then.

So I do understand that the news brings up more than a question about property. It brings back people at different ages, and visits that cannot be repeated, and a time when Tom was there. I have those memories as well. Making this decision has not meant that I have stopped feeling them.

Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. It took me a long time to believe that for myself. At first I could probably have said it to somebody else more readily than I could have acted on it.

There is no single day I can point to when it all became clear. There was the regular driving, the work, the fall, the roof survey, and the gradual understanding that I was not going to find it easier by leaving the decision for another year. I had to decide what I could manage now, rather than what I wished I could still manage.

What I got wrong was keeping so much of that thinking to myself.

Declan heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp, not from me. He should never have heard it that way. There is no blame on Gráinne for that. I had left a gap where a conversation with me ought to have been, and the news reached him through it.

He rang me at two in the morning his time. He was very upset. During that call he said I was “selling Dad”, and I said things back that I should not have said.

I am not going to set down the rest of that conversation here. It would do neither of us any good, and this is not an invitation for the family to choose a side. But I cannot give you an honest account while leaving out the fact that I hurt him, or making it sound as though the difficulty was only that he did not like my decision.

I regret not consulting you, Declan. You should have heard from me what I was thinking, what the survey had found, and how I was managing. You should have had a chance to speak to me before the sale was agreed. I was wrong not to give you that chance.

Consulting you would not necessarily have meant that we agreed. I have to be honest about that too. I am not willing to wait until your summer visit to sell the house. I cannot keep taking care of it until then, and I do not want to carry the responsibility for another winter and spring in the hope that the decision might feel easier later.

The sale is going ahead. I know that makes the conversation I should have had with you impossible to recover in its proper form. I cannot now offer you a say beforehand. I can only acknowledge that you should have had one, and listen to what you want to say now without treating your hurt as an inconvenience.

I’m sorry for how you found out, and I’m sorry for the things I said on the phone. I am not sorry for deciding to sell. That may be difficult to read, but I would rather say it honestly than offer an apology which sounds as though I am promising to change my mind.

I’m not angry with you. You don’t have to agree with me before we can speak again. My door is open, and I would like us to talk.

To the rest of the family, I am sorry too if you heard this second-hand, or felt that something important had been decided and you were being told after everybody else. I understand why that would hurt. I delayed telling people something difficult, and in doing so I made it more difficult. I don’t have a better explanation than that.

There are things from the house which are staying with the family, and I want everyone to know what they are.

The dresser is going to Úna’s. We are keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. They are not going with the sale.

I know those things are not a substitute for the house. I don’t expect somebody who is grieving the loss of Glenmore as our family place to be cheered up simply because the dresser is safe. But they matter, and knowing where they are matters. I want the photographs kept, and the names and stories that go with them remembered, not left for somebody years from now to try to work out.

The Joyces have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. I am grateful to them for that. We will, of course, remember that it is their home and be considerate. Their kindness doesn’t mean nothing is changing. But it does mean that selling need not be the last time any of us walks there.

Before the house is cleared, I would like us to have a family day there on **Sunday 13 December**. Anyone who can come is welcome. We’ll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies.

I know not everyone can make a journey in December, particularly those of you abroad. Please don’t read this as a test of who cares enough to come. I would love to have you there, but I know what travelling involves, and I know a date put on a blog does not make everybody free to travel.

For those who can come, I don’t want it to be a formal occasion. We can eat, walk about, look at the photographs and spend some time in the place together. If you can help with the names or occasions in the photographs, all the better. There are always things one person remembers that another has forgotten, or never knew.

Nobody has to arrive cheerful about the sale. Nobody has to tell me I have done the right thing. I would like us to be together there while it is still possible, rather than let these last weeks go by with all our conversations happening separately on the phone.

Declan, that invitation is for you as much as for anyone, if you can manage it. And if you cannot, the invitation to talk is there all the same.

For clarity, once more: **the sale closes on 15 January 2027**. I have agreed to sell to Aoife and Kevin Joyce, who intend to make it their family home. The dresser, fiddle, photographs, Sacred Heart lamp and gate sign are being kept.

I am sad about selling Glenmore. I am also relieved that I will not have to keep looking after it, and I have found that harder to admit than the sadness. Both are true. I loved Tom, I love the history we have in that house, and I cannot maintain it any longer.

I hope, in time, those of you who are hurt by this will understand why I have done it. I don’t expect one post to settle everybody’s feelings, or to make up for the conversations I should have had. But at least you have heard it from me now, in full.

I’d love to see as many of you as can come on the 13th. Soup, sandwiches and wellies. We’ll have plenty to talk about.
